events.excerpt: Two arXiv v1 preprints, SwarmEvolve and Scientist World , measure different research-agent tasks : evolutionary program search and performance in paper-derived environments. Throughput and Evolutionary Search SwarmEvolve, authored by Qile Jiang and George Em Karniadakis, focuses on the efficiency of evolutionary program search. The system operates by deploying 10 swarms, each containing 45 latent agents per round. To maintain diversity, a novelty filter keeps 30 agents in each swarm; summarizers read their KV caches to synthesize candidate programs. This mechanism is tested across 21 mathematical and scientific-computing problems. The researchers tested Qwen3 8B, 14B and 32B-FP8 models, using three seeds and 60-minute runs on one GPU with eight CPU cores. Against OpenEvolve, ShinkaEvolve and CodeEvolve, the authors report the highest average score across all three model sizes, 5 to 13 times more programs evaluated per hour, and median times of 3 to 8 minutes to reach the baselines’ 60-minute scores. The reported measures combine program quality with search throughput: one describes results, the other the number of candidate programs the system can evaluate under the fixed time budget. events.excerpt: NCCL 2.32.3 added TLS 1.3 PSK encryption of its TCP sockets via the process-global ncclSetEncryption . PyTorch has no way to enable it. Adds ProcessGroupNCCL.Options.encryption_psk , honored by nccl2 (which shares the Options class); legacy ProcessGroupNCCL (including shrink) rejects it and torchcomms (including split) raises instead of silently ignoring it. NCCL rereads the key for every new socket, including live communicators', so nccl2 applies it once in the constructor of the first group: later groups (including split children) must pass the same key or none, and a different key or a key on a non-first group raises. Mismatched keys across ranks can hang, as NCCL drops failed handshakes. NCCL validates length (>= 32 bytes); NUL bytes raise ValueError. NCCL < 2.32.3 and ROCm raise. NCCL builds without TLS (PyPI wheels, CI) accept the key and fail at communicator init. split / shrink children inherit the key; if a child can't apply its key, the already-created child comm is aborted and the error raised (validation can't precede the collective without hanging other ranks). Groups constructed with a key must not be constructed concurrently with other groups (documented, no new lock). TORCH_NCCL_ENCRYPTION_PSK (nccl2 only) supplies the key when encryption_psk is unset and no key h

events.excerpt: OpenAI, Microsoft, and CrowdStrike are taking steps to limit the capabilities of AI agents that act outside their parameters of operation. OpenAI has a way of stopping output from a research model. CrowdStrike stops agents from accessing AI models. Microsoft limits the action that an AI agent can perform. However, an agent might retain access to other tools, credentials or network connections that these safeguards do not cover. What OpenAI’s Control Room can and can’t stop On November 9, OpenAI explained how Control Room functions. The system is currently in use in the company’s research infrastructure and is responsible for tracking any jobs that need AI-generated outputs. Whenever a person or an automatic monitor puts the job on hold, Control Room causes the model to stop issuing outputs in as little as 35 seconds. The 35 seconds does not include the time necessary for detecting the problem. The timer only begins after Control Room receives a stop order. The research job might still be running, and no earlier actions can be undone. The delay happens due to the caching system being used for authorization. The company is working to eliminate this delay. CrowdStrike and Microsoft take the enterprise route On November 3, CrowdStrike introduced AI Kill Switch through its Falcon Guar

events.excerpt: There are a lot of things you can do with an Xserver, but run it on a microcontroller? Well, if that microcontroller is an ESP32-S3, [Sergey Zorin]– and Claude– have got you covered with Woodland X11 , a full-featured port of everyone’s favourite XServer. Now, it is just the core Xserver with no extensions, and currently targeted specifically at the Elecrow CrowPanel Advance 4.3″, a device that packages an ESP32-S3-N16R8 with an 800×480 RGB565 IPS panel and GT911 touch. In this implementation, your finger is the Xcursor. There’s even two-finger scroll implemented, though no keyboard. As you can see in the demo video embedded below, it works well enough for those oldschool X applications like xclock, xcalc and– crucially!– xeyes. What’s the point of an Xserver without googly eyes, anyway? In reality, you’re not likely to set this up just for Xeyes, but the idea of having bringing Linux applications to a little display via WiFi or — as in the video– wired connection has no limit of use cases. Try that with Wayland ! Considering X11’s vintage, it is perhaps not surprising that it fits on the ESP32-S3, a chip we’ve seen emulate an entire 386 PC before– a PC that could run an Xserver, for you youngun’s. Thanks to [Sergey] for the tip!
events.headline: X Window System on the ESP32

events.excerpt: The US Federal Aviation Administration on Friday issued an advisory that prevented the takeoff of flights in US airspace for around five hours, creating chaos for travelers and airports. The stop was finally lifted around 8:30 PM Eastern Time, but only after thousands of flights were canceled or delayed, leaving travelers stranded. The FAA has not yet confirmed a reason for the stop. Original story below: "The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers," said US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy in a statement. "FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them." A spokesperson at the FAA press office reached by phone said he was unable to provide further information. And an email response from the agency repeated Duffy's statement. The FAA ATCSCC advisory halts departing flights and says international flights will be dealt with individually. The notice says, "Due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety. Attention all aircraft operators, by order of the Federal Aviation Command Center all airports are ground stopped. All departing traffic should remain stopped until further notice. events.excerpt: Taiwanese chipmaking giant TSMC has confirmed a leak of personal information belonging to some current and former employees. Reports from the local media said anonymous sellers on underground forums, including DarkForums and BreachForums, offered around 46,000 employee records for 3 Bitcoin. TSMC Employee Data Leak The sellers also threatened to make the data public if no buyer came forward within a week. TSMC confirmed that employee information had appeared on external websites but maintained that there was no evidence its own systems had been breached. The company also said the incident did not affect customer information or production-related data. According to TSMC, the exposed records were linked to a cloud service provider, although it has not identified the provider or explained what service it handled. Business Next reported that samples shared on the forums contained names, national ID numbers, and bank account details. TSMC said affected individuals have already been notified and that it is working with the service provider, cybersecurity firms and law enforcement to investigate where the leak originated. events.headline: TSMC Confirms Employee Data Leak as Hackers Try to Sell 46,000 Records for Bitcoin

events.excerpt: On October 29, in about twenty minutes, $6.3 billion left Binance’s wallets. The largest crypto theft in history, more than four times the Bybit hack of February 2025. The entry point, according to the exchange itself, was an engineer’s computer, infected after a fake job interview. Two days later, Binance announced it had restored 98% of the assets with its own funds; the next day, it resumed withdrawals. Hold on to that last fact. It’s the most important one, and the least talked about. To a Man with a Hammer, Every Problem Looks Like a Nail Mt. Gox, 2014 . QuadrigaCX, 2019. FTX, 2022. Bybit, 2025. Binance, 2026, to name just the most notorious. Different problems, always the same answer: self-custody, because, after all, not your keys, not your coins . The premise is technically true. If you don’t hold the private key, you don’t control the asset: you have a claim against whoever does. The conclusion usually drawn from it isn’t that self-custody is, necessarily, safer.
